wire.title: Footbridge collapses at Harrow Ford as commuters cross the Tamsin

paragraphs.text: A pedestrian footbridge over the River Tamsin collapsed in Harrow Ford on Tuesday evening, sending commuters and cyclists into the water, emergency services said.
The Ledgerwood Bridge, a steel and timber walkway built in 1964, gave way at about 6:10 pm as the evening rush hour crossed from the railway station to the market district.
Northgate Rescue Service said crews from four stations reached the river within 11 minutes and pulled people from the water and from the broken deck.
People were taken to Harrow General Hospital with injuries ranging from cuts and bruises to suspected broken bones, a hospital spokeswoman said.
Witnesses described a loud crack followed by a section of the deck dropping away. “It just folded in the middle,” said a cyclist who had crossed seconds earlier.
The river was running higher than usual after three days of rain, and rescuers worked from boats and from the bank with ropes and lights as darkness fell.
Police closed Station Road, Mill Street and the riverside path, and asked the public to avoid the area so ambulances could reach the scene.
Harrow Borough Council said the bridge had been inspected in March and had been due for repairs to its eastern bearings next spring.
Councillor Ines Valmont, who leads the council, said her thoughts were with those hurt and that an independent investigation would begin at once.
The rail line between Southgate and Marlow was suspended for several hours while engineers checked the nearby viaduct.
Trains resumed at about 11 pm with delays of up to 25 minutes, the operator, Tamsin Valley Rail, said.
The bridge opened in 1964 and carries an estimated 9,000 crossings on a typical weekday, according to council figures.
It was strengthened in 1998 after a survey found corrosion in several of its steel hangers, and a further survey was carried out in March.
Engineers from the firm Alder & Pike, which carried out the March inspection, said they were working with investigators and would not comment on the cause.
The Rail and Marine Safety Board said it had sent a team of three investigators to Harrow Ford and would publish an interim note within 30 days.
A reception centre was opened at the Ledgerwood Community Hall for families looking for relatives, and a helpline was set up.
The helpline is being run by the council and police, and relatives were asked not to travel to the hospital unless contacted.
Traders on Mill Street said customers were turned away after the closure, and the weekly market due on Thursday has been moved to Saturday.
Schools in Harrow Ford will open as normal, though some buses are on diversion, the county education office said.
The Environment Agency said the river level was being monitored and that no further flood warnings were in force for the Tamsin valley.
Divers searched the river bed overnight to confirm that nobody remained in the water, and the search was formally stood down at dawn.
The council said it would publish the inspection reports for the bridge once the investigators agreed they could be released.
Fenwick Wire will update this report as more information becomes available.

wire.title: Kessel Valley line to close for six weeks of bridge repairs

paragraphs.text: The Kessel Valley railway line will close for six weeks from 3 November while engineers repair a damaged bridge near Harrow Bridge station, the operator said on Monday.
The line carries about 1,200 commuters a day between Harrow Bridge and the coast, and replacement buses will run every 20 minutes during the closure.
Kessel Rail said the bridge had been damaged by flooding in September and that inspections had found erosion around two of its supports.
The operator apologised for the disruption and said the work could not be put off without risking a longer closure in the depths of winter.
Season ticket holders will be offered a refund for the weeks the line is shut, the company said, with details to be published on its website.
Local MP Dana Whitlow said she had asked the transport department to make sure replacement services were accessible for disabled passengers.

wire.title: Fire guts Port Alder warehouse; twelve treated for smoke inhalation

paragraphs.text: A fire tore through a storage warehouse on the Port Alder industrial estate late on Sunday, sending a column of black smoke over the harbour and forcing the closure of two nearby roads.
Twelve people were treated for smoke inhalation after the fire at the Port Alder warehouse, officials said. None of the injuries were described as life-threatening.
At least 40 firefighters were sent to the scene from Port Alder and three neighbouring towns, and the blaze took 6 hours to bring under control.
The warehouse, owned by the logistics firm Brennock Freight, held packaging materials and household goods awaiting shipment to retailers across the region.
Residents within half a mile of the site were told to keep windows and doors closed overnight while crews dampened down hot spots.
Investigators have not yet said what caused the fire. A spokesperson for the regional fire service said an inquiry would begin once the building was declared safe to enter.
Harbour Road and Quay Lane remained closed on Monday morning, and the town council advised drivers to use the coast road instead.
Brennock Freight said in a statement that all of its staff on the night shift had been accounted for and thanked emergency crews for their response.

quiet.title: Why your afternoon coffee might be costing you sleep

paragraphs.text: Most adults should aim for seven to nine hours of sleep a night, yet surveys keep finding that a large share of us regularly get less than that.
Caffeine can stay in your system for up to six hours, which means a mid-afternoon coffee may still be working when you are trying to fall asleep.
Sleep researchers often describe caffeine as borrowing alertness from later in the day, because it blocks the chemical signal that builds up as you get tired.
Keeping a regular wake-up time, even at weekends, is one of the simplest habits for steadier sleep, and it costs nothing to try.
If you want to cut back, reduce your intake gradually over a week or two rather than stopping all at once, to avoid headaches.
